question: When does a traveller start shortening prayers: at home, at the airport, or once outside the city?
answer:
Second point: when does qasr begin? Once you've decided it is qasr for me — so this Friday I'm going to Atlanta, clearly there is qasr for me — when will qasr begin? When I pack my bags? I'm about to leave for the airport, it's dhuhr time. Can I start my qasr, knowing I'm stepping out the door and I'm heading to the airport? I'll say, let me just do qasr and jama', dhuhr and asr, get it out of the way. Can I do qasr from my house? How about if I get to the plane, and I'm waiting, and it's almost maghrib time — oh, let me just pray dhuhr and asr on the plane — but I'm still in my city? When does qasr begin?

So again, as you can imagine, there are a number of opinions. However, the overwhelming majority of the Sahaba and Tabi'un had one opinion. So alhamdulillah, we can say in this case we have a vast majority who says: **safar begins when you travel outside of the walls of the city.** When you leave the final habitations of the city, and your back is to the city and you're walking away, you're going out — even if you can still see the city — you have left the premises of your land. Not your country, but your city.

And there are numerous narrations from the Sahaba themselves. Of them is that some of the Sahaba would break their fast in Ramadan when they were going on a long journey. You're not going to fast that day, but they're fasting when they wake up. You cannot just wake up in Ramadan and say, oh, I have a safar at 6 a.m. — let's say 2 p.m. — I'm not going to fast today. No, you are in Ramadan; you are not a musafir. Now imagine in those days: you're walking at 7 a.m., you're not going to be able to fast, you know you're going to break your fast, but you are still starting in Ramadan. You're going to be fasting.

Some of the Sahaba, when they walked outside the city, one of them said to his servant, 'Okay, give me the water now. Give me something now to break. I have a long day ahead; we're going to break the fast anyway.' And his servant said, 'I can see the walls of the city.' He said, 'Doesn't matter, give it to me now. We're in safar now.' The safar is done. Even if you can see the walls of the city, you have left the premises.

Now, in those days they had walls. In our times there is no wall. So you have to use a bit of a cultural thing, because habitation goes smaller and smaller; you get to smaller and smaller places. But there is still something called the overall city of Dallas. And it's not an exact line, but you get the point: when you have left and you feel that, okay, now I am no longer in my city of residence, then safar can begin. And that is when you can start your qasr.

And this is proven actually in a hadith of Anas ibn Malik, that he said: we prayed dhuhr four rak'ahs in Medina — this is going for Hajj — then when we got to Dhul Hulayfah, we prayed two rak'ahs. Dhul Hulayfah is literally a 10-minute drive from Medina. It's definitely not four burud or 16 farsakh. Not at all. Dhul Hulayfah is 10 minutes; those of you that have done Umrah from Medina, you know this. Dhul Hulayfah is literally outside, but it is outside the city. So Anas says, in Medina we prayed four; when we got to Dhul Hulayfah we prayed two. Even though you haven't gone the distance — even if you followed the four burud or whatever positions, you're still within that — safar has begun.

So when does safar begin? It begins when you leave the area, the city you inhabit. This is the second point.
